title: Krishna Vanishes
story:
It began on a night when the moon rose full and calm over Vrindavan, painting every corner of the sky with its red light, the way a beloved long away brightens a face at the moment of return. The forest took the light softly — the leaves, the paths, the water of the Yamuna all touched with that red glow — and it was a night made for beauty and for longing. When Krishna's flute sounded through the forest, the women of Vraja heard it in the middle of their ordinary tasks and set them down. One left off milking, another left the milk half-boiled over the fire, another turned from a husband she was serving, another from a child she was feeding — and they came, each one slipping away unnoticed, their earrings swinging as they hurried to where their beloved stood. Some came with their clothes and ornaments half arranged, so great was their haste; and some who found themselves shut inside their houses, unable to slip out, stood where they were and closed their eyes and held him in their minds. Their families called them back, but they did not turn. Their minds were no longer their own; Krishna had taken them, and the women went where the music led.

He received them, and for a while the forest held only what they had all come for. It is easy, in such a moment, for a small and secret thought to take root: that the joy is theirs, that they have earned it, that the one they love is somehow their own.

The verses put it plainly. Pride rose in the gopis out of their good fortune — the sense that they, of all people, possessed him. It was a small thing, the way such pride always begins: a certain warmth in the heart, a certain sense of having been chosen. And Krishna saw it.

There was no word, no warning. Where he had been, there was nothing. He vanished then and there, in the middle of the night, in the middle of their happiness, leaving the women he loved standing suddenly alone among the trees.

But the verses are careful to say why. He did not leave them to punish them. He left them to humble them, and to favor them. The pride that had begun to grow in them was the one thing that could have spoiled what they had found; and so the Lord, who had come so close, stepped back, so that what they felt for him could grow deeper than the thing they felt for themselves.

In the silence he left behind, the night was suddenly very large, and the gopis understood, in a way they had not understood before, how much of what they loved was simply him. The flute had stopped. The place where he had stood still held the warmth of him, and that was all that was left. They looked at one another in the red moonlight, and none of them could speak. They had asked the night for so much, and the night had given it, and now, in an instant, it had been taken back — not to hurt them, but to teach them what it was they had been given. The moon had not dimmed, and the forest had not changed. Only he was gone; and without him, the same night was a different place.
reflection: Krishna's disappearance is the opposite of abandonment. He removes the one thing — pride — that would have soured the gopis' love, so that what remains is only the love itself.
hero_scene: A full moon rising red over the Vrindavan forest at night, and the gopis standing suddenly alone among dark trees, turning to find the space where Krishna stood a moment before now empty.
